title: Behind Every Great School
author: mrsk04
summary: Written as a summer reflection, this essay honors the principals who shaped the author across two decades of teaching — exploring, through specific remembered relationships, what great school leadership actually looks like in practice rather than theory. The author traces three distinct leadership eras, each embodied by a different principal: an early mentor who hired her sight unseen and modeled daily the three values she named aloud (Respect, Responsibility, Integrity) until they were indistinguishable from the school's culture; a later leader who created a genuinely collaborative professional environment in which teachers felt protected and trusted; and a final leader whose visible dedication to students over adults set the standard by which everything else was measured. The article is not a list of leadership qualities but a demonstration of how those qualities are transmitted through relationship — through what the principal notices, what she names, what she does publicly versus privately, and what she protects. The piece is particularly valuable as a meditation on how leaders shape teachers, and therefore students, through their daily embodiment of priorities rather than through direction.
points: The most powerful form of leadership modeling is not stated in PD sessions or mission documents but enacted daily in visible behaviors that make values unmistakable — the principal who repeats 'Respect, Responsibility, Integrity' on the voicemail until it is simply what the school is.

Great principals shape teachers, and thereby students, far more than any curriculum or professional development program: the author traces the person she became as a teacher directly to the leaders who trusted her, challenged her, and publicly stood behind her.

Trust as a leadership tool is concrete, not abstract: it looks like a principal who assumes good faith when a teacher makes a questionable choice, who deals with parent complaints by backing the teacher first, and who treats the professional relationship as one of mutual accountability rather than supervision.

The leader who prioritizes students over adult comfort creates a different institutional culture: when staff sees the leader make decisions that are harder for adults but better for students, the implicit message is that everyone's decisions should clear the same bar.

The essay's most transferable insight is what schools lose when leaders cycle too quickly: the principals who made the most difference were each present long enough to allow culture to accumulate through consistency, and the author's development as a teacher tracked closely with those periods of stability.
quotes: Summer is a time for reflection for me, and lately the need for great leadership in schools has been at the top of my mind. So this post is for the leaders who made me, and every teacher they’ve worked with, a better teacher.

She had a clear vision, clear expectations for what good teaching looked like, clear standards for what kids should be doing and learning. But, and this is the part so many leaders miss, she backed those expectations with the time, support and tools to meet them.
She had promised to balance classrooms if I stayed in 4th instead of moving down to 3rd. But the new hire didn’t have gifted-and-talented certification.

In observations, she’d sit in the back of the classroom with an absolutely unreadable face, and I’d spend the whole lesson spiraling. But that was the thing: she actually watched, and she actually paid attention.

I avoid it like the plague, and if I’m honest, that single trait alone probably cancels out any other quality I have that might make me good in the role. But in her ever-reassuring way, she insisted I had the right skill set and spent the following two years encouraging me to move beyond the classroom.

Declining enrollment hit this school hard, and once again I had to leave a school and community I loved, despite my principal’s best attempts to advocate to keep me. Year 20: All of the Above Before landing here, I feared education had turned into something that wasn’t sustainable, and that the leaders of the past were just that.

They made sure every child could say out loud, “I feel safe and seen here,” and mean it, not just say it because it was expected. And these women, who I am so lucky to have had in my life, were the great ones.
